title: Boyd's name on the arrangements
summary: Boyd stamped his name on arrangements, and a story tells of a pitiful chart he wrote himself.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I guess this shouldn't be the last reference to Boyd, but it's something I neglected to mention and I think it's incredibly important and terribly significant, every piece of paper I have on that library is either handwritten or rubber stamped, a Boyd Raeburn arrangement. It's there indiscriminately on your work, on Johnny's work--
Well, that shows you what happened to Boyd as a result of all this.
On the back of one of those record jackets over there, that not for sale jacket, the jazz of 1945 or '46, whatever it was, it says, one of the arrangers is Boyd Raeburn.

I was told about a Boyd arrangement once. This was after the band had come to New York, perhaps a year after I had left it, maybe two years after I left it, somewhere in that period, I was told by one of the guys that was on the band, it may have been Frank Socolow, it was one of the saxophone players, told me one of the most amazing stories, to me; that they had a rehearsal and Boyd walked in with a chart that he had written and he put it on the stand and rehearsed it, and I was--you know, tell me, what was it like and he said it was pitiful.
A child with the least amount of talent would have written something better than what he had done. It was bad, infantile. It was ghastly. And they laughed at him. But so much for his writing.
But he did start planning to be responsible for the writing.
Yeah, the reference to that, of course, is not really claiming responsibility or claiming credit, but I would gather some sort of insecurity--why would you think he would swing that way?
I can only guess that maybe he didn't enjoy the feeling of not being responsible for something important, that seemed to be happening with his orchestra.

Woody, on the other hand, advertised the fact that he was only the editor, he was proud of the fact--McKenney has salvaged the phrase 'musical idiot' which you may have in some of that material I sent you, Boyd once said, for a musical idiot, I've got

a great band.
Woody always kind of--he would never use that word, but always suggested that gee, I was a great editor, I think, and allowed my guys to have a good band. It's always made him sort of a hero for saying it. Enough of that, I guess.
I told you that I was going to talk more on this than any interviewer really should. I'm saying that to Morgenstern.
